text.p: Breastfeeding mothers infected with the AIDS virus should wean their babies as soon as they can feed them safely by other means, researchers working in Africa said on Friday.

For many of the Third World's poor, they said, the best choice would be weaning at about six months, when the child can take solid food and the chances that it is not yet infected were found to be unexpectedly good.

Long-standing advice that "breast is best" stands for most of the Third World because formula feeding carries a high risk of other diseases spread by unclean water, one of the researchers, Kevin De Cock of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told Reuters.
"Setting policy about breastfeeding in areas of high rates of HIV infection is a trade-off," De Cock said in a telephone interview.
"If you encourage women who are HIV-infected not to breastfeed then you raise the risk of infant mortality from diarrhoeal disease, infection, et cetera," he said.
But HIV mothers with clear access to clean water who could follow instructions on preparing clean formula should be advised to do so, he said

And while any HIV mother who breastfeeds takes the risk of infecting her baby, the new research by Ehounou Ekpini of Projet RETRO-CI in Ivory Coast and a team including De Cock showed that the transmission often took place at a relatively late stage.
If weaning before six months is not a safe option, it is still best to do it then rather than later, the researchers said.
"Our results indicate that the risk of transmission through breastfeeding does not disappear after the first few weeks of life, but continues throughout the entire breastfeeding period."
The advice was based on a study of several hundred mothers and children.
Most of the mothers, 138, were infected with HIV-1 before giving birth, 132 had the less-virulent HIV-2 and 69 had both. They were compared to 274 uninfected women.
By six months of age, 28 percent of children born to HIV-1 positive mothers and 18 percent of those born to mothers infected with both viruses were infected, too.
Another 12 percent of babies born to HIV-1 infected mothers and six percent of those born to mothers with both infections became HIV-positive after six months, they said.
"Our...results show that all but one of the children in whom late postnatal transmission occurred were uninfected at six months of age," they wrote.
"Our results suggest that to wean children at roughly six months of age could reduce the risk of HIV transmission through breastfeeding."
